label: Sentence Boundaries
overview: Sentence boundary questions test whether you can recognize and correct run-on sentences, comma splices, and sentence fragments. SAT questions ask you to choose the punctuation or conjunction that correctly joins or separates independent clauses. The core rule: two independent clauses cannot be joined by only a comma — you need a period, semicolon, or coordinating conjunction.

workedExamples.problem: Choose the best option: 'The experiment was a success _____ the team celebrated.'  (A) ,  (B) ;  (C) because  (D) , so

steps.title: Identify both clauses
steps.content: 'The experiment was a success' and 'the team celebrated' are both independent clauses (each has a subject and verb and can stand alone).

steps.title: Test each option
steps.content: (A) comma alone — comma splice, incorrect. (B) semicolon — grammatically correct but doesn't show the cause-effect relationship. (D) comma + 'so' — correct: FANBOYS conjunction showing result.

steps.title: Choose the best answer
steps.content: (D) 'The experiment was a success, so the team celebrated.' conveys meaning and is grammatically correct.

commonMistakes.mistake: Thinking a semicolon and a comma are interchangeable
commonMistakes.fix: A semicolon can join two independent clauses alone. A comma can only join them when followed by a coordinating conjunction (FANBOYS: for, and, nor, but, or, yet, so).

commonMistakes.mistake: Treating a dependent clause as an independent clause
commonMistakes.fix: A dependent clause (starting with 'because,' 'although,' 'when,' etc.) cannot stand alone. It must be attached to an independent clause — no semicolon between them.

quickTip: FANBOYS = For, And, Nor, But, Or, Yet, So. Only these seven coordinating conjunctions (with a comma) can join two independent clauses in a simple comma construction.
